A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the expanded title and renumbered supplementary sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original HumanML3D and KIT-ML experiments, including generation benchmarks, diagnostic experiments, ablations, reconstruction results, and model-scaling results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds noise-schedule tests, component and baseline-reformulation analyses, and original-evaluator results.

M1.justification: The essential-feature autoencoder, masked autoregressive transformer, diffusion MLPs, noise/velocity objectives, and sampling procedures remain unchanged. Clarifications about pseudo-ordering and masked prediction explain the existing method; the new ablations do not establish a revised proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions use HumanML3D and KIT-ML for text-to-motion generation and retain the temporal-editing discussion. The added diagnostic experiments reuse HumanML3D without introducing another dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: The main benchmark comparator set in Table 5 is unchanged. The original-evaluator comparison expands to include MMM in v2 Table A4, alongside MDM, T2M-GPT, and MoMask already compared under that evaluator in Table 4.

E3.justification: The main splits, training budgets, and benchmark protocol remain unchanged. Added experiments introduce linear-schedule noise prediction for MDM, essential-only and latent baseline configurations, prediction-target controls, and output conversion for original-evaluator testing (Tables 2 and A2-A4).

E4.justification: New Tables A2-A4 separate feature removal from autoencoding, test whether representation changes benefit existing diffusion baselines, compare prediction targets, and examine conversion-induced evaluation bias. Table 2 adds a noise-schedule check, while Section 2.2 quantifies codebook uniformity. These substantially extend v1's diagnostic and ablation evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 evaluations and 95% confidence intervals for the main benchmarks. The added diagnostic tables use point estimates, consistent with earlier ablation reporting; no new seed, replication, or uncertainty-estimation procedure is specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial diagnostic results, including linear-schedule MDM FID 1.574, the essential-only autoregressive variant's FID 0.657, latent MDM FID 0.327, and original-evaluator FID 0.061 for the proposed method. Codebook KL divergences are also added. Table 5 and the matched reconstruction, scaling, and timing results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation (4) restores missing square roots, changing the squared-error multiplier from ((1-alpha_bar_t)/alpha_bar_t)^2 to (1-alpha_bar_t)/alpha_bar_t. This agrees with the derivation already present in Appendix A.1; no new proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claims remain diagnosing representation and evaluation biases, proposing scalable masked autoregressive diffusion, and achieving strong performance on HumanML3D and KIT-ML. Removing 'bidirectional' from headline descriptions does not change the method's scope: bidirectional attention remains explicit in Section 3.2.2.

C2.justification: Appendix D.3 newly discusses conversion errors, one-frame loss, and MoMask reproduction discrepancies when interpreting original-evaluator results. The added analyses distinguish benefits of essential features and latent encoding. The existing generation-speed limitation is retained.

D1.justification: The implementation appendix retains the architecture, optimizer, batch sizes, learning-rate schedules, and guidance scales. v2 newly identifies the earlier MDM noise-prediction setting as using a cosine schedule and documents conversion through joints back to HumanML3D representations, including the lost frame.

R1.justification: New Appendix B substantially expands coverage of earlier motion-language alignment, diffusion and VQ methods, control, interactions, and other motion applications. It adds discussion of concurrent ScaMo and explicitly positions the proposed autoregression against prior motion-diffusion approaches using prefix conditioning.

P1.justification: v2 extends the title, edits prose, and clarifies masking, pseudo-ordering, and evaluation. It adds a detailed related-work appendix and named supplementary analysis subsections while preserving the main section sequence and much of the existing text.

P2.justification: v2 adds appendix Tables A2-A4 and a row to Table 2, adjusts Figure 1 labeling, resizes Figure 4, and relocates Figure 3. Earlier scaling and timing tables are retained as A5 and A6. The basic figure designs and two-column layout remain.

improvement.justification: v1's generation ablation bundled feature removal with autoencoding, and its proposed model was benchmarked only with the replacement evaluators. v2 Tables A2-A4 separate these effects, test representation changes on baselines, and add original-evaluator comparisons with conversion controls. These additions substantially strengthen attribution and comparison transparency. The equation correction also improves consistency, although the new diagnostic tables still lack uncertainty estimates.
